```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
from _lib.orplot import COLORS
from _lib.toy_network import ARCS, NODES, POS, CAP, max_flow_steps, draw_network

steps = max_flow_steps()
final = steps[-1]
S = final["cut"]
cut_arcs = [(u, v) for u, v, *_ in ARCS if u in S and v not in S]
```

## The idea

Now the arcs have **capacities**: at most $u_{ij}$ units per hour can travel along arc
$(i, j)$. How much can be sent from a source $s$ to a sink $t$ in total, if flow is
conserved at every other node (what comes in goes out)?

A natural upper bound comes from **cuts**. Split the nodes into a set $S$ containing $s$
and its complement containing $t$. Every unit of flow must cross from $S$ to the other
side somewhere, so the flow can never exceed the total capacity of the arcs leaving
$S$. The remarkable fact is that the **smallest** such bound is always achieved.

In the toy network the maximum flow is $18$, and the cut $S = \{s, a, b\}$, whose
outgoing arcs $a \to c$, $a \to d$, $b \to d$ have capacities $6 + 4 + 8 = 18$, proves
that no more is possible.

```{python}
#| label: fig-maxflow
#| fig-cap: "A maximum flow of value 18 in the toy network; each arc shows flow / capacity. The green nodes form the source side $S = \\{s, a, b\\}$ of a minimum cut. The red arcs leave $S$; they are all full, and their capacities add up to 18. No arc enters $S$ with positive flow. That certifies that 18 is the maximum."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.7))
draw_network(ax, label="flow", flow=final["flow"], highlight=cut_arcs,
             node_color={v: "#a6d8a8" for v in S})
plt.show()
```

## The math

### Flows and cuts

A **flow** assigns $x_{ij}$ to each arc with $0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}$ and conservation
at every node other than $s$ and $t$. Its **value** is the net amount leaving $s$. An
**$s$–$t$ cut** is a set $S$ of nodes with $s \in S$, $t \notin S$, and its
**capacity** is the total capacity of arcs from $S$ to outside $S$.

For any flow $x$ and any cut $S$,
$$
\text{value}(x) \;=\; \sum_{\text{arcs out of } S} x_{ij} \;-\; \sum_{\text{arcs into } S} x_{ij}
\;\le\; \text{capacity}(S).
$$
(The flow that leaves $S$, minus what comes back, is what $s$ sent; and arc flows are at
most their capacities and at least zero.)

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (max-flow min-cut)
The maximum value of an $s$–$t$ flow equals the minimum capacity of an $s$–$t$ cut.
:::

The theorem was proved in 1956 independently by @ford1956a and by @elias1956. It is
[LP duality](../../linear-programming/duality/lp-duality.qmd) for the max-flow LP, but
it has a direct combinatorial proof that also gives an algorithm.

### Augmenting paths

Given a current flow, the **residual network** says how the flow can still be changed:

- an arc $(i, j)$ with $x_{ij} < u_{ij}$ can carry $u_{ij} - x_{ij}$ more (forward);
- an arc $(i, j)$ with $x_{ij} > 0$ can have up to $x_{ij}$ of its flow cancelled, which
  acts like sending flow from $j$ back to $i$ (backward).

An **augmenting path** is an $s$–$t$ path in the residual network. Pushing the smallest
residual capacity along it (the **bottleneck**) increases the flow value. The
augmenting-path algorithm of @ford1957 repeats this until no augmenting path is left.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (optimality of augmenting paths)
A flow is maximum if and only if there is no augmenting path. In that case, the set $S$
of nodes reachable from $s$ in the residual network is a minimum cut.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (integrality)
If all capacities are integers, there is a maximum flow in which every arc flow is an
integer, and the augmenting-path algorithm finds one.
:::

The integrality theorem is what makes flows so useful for combinatorial problems:
"route a whole number of trucks", "assign each worker to one job". The LP happens to have
integer optimal solutions, so no integer programming is needed. The
[total unimodularity](../integrality-and-matching/total-unimodularity.qmd) page explains why.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
mfChart = {
  const R = mf[mfStep], C = mfColors, W = 640, H = 380;
  const x = d3.scaleLinear([-0.35, 3.55], [10, W - 10]);
  const y = d3.scaleLinear([-0.45, 2.45], [H - 10, 10]);
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, W, H])
      .style("width", "100%").style("max-width", "680px")
      .style("font-family", "inherit").style("font-size", "16px");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  for (const [id, col] of [["mf-n", "currentColor"], ["mf-p", C.weak], ["mf-c", C.hull]])
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10").attr("refX", 9)
      .attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 6).attr("markerHeight", 6)
      .attr("orient", "auto-start-reverse").append("path")
      .attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10Z").attr("fill", col);
  const onPath = (u, v) => R.path && R.path.some(p => p[0] === u && p[1] === v);
  const dirOf = (u, v) => R.path.find(p => p[0] === u && p[1] === v)[2];
  const inCut = (u, v) => R.cut && R.cut.includes(u) && !R.cut.includes(v);
  if (R.cut) for (const v of R.cut)
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x(mfPos[v][0])).attr("cy", y(mfPos[v][1])).attr("r", 30)
       .attr("fill", C.hull).attr("fill-opacity", 0.25);
  mfArcs.forEach(([u, v, k], j) => {
    const p = mfPos[u], q = mfPos[v];
    const dx = x(q[0]) - x(p[0]), dy = y(q[1]) - y(p[1]), L = Math.hypot(dx, dy);
    const ux = dx / L, uy = dy / L, r = 22;
    const hl = onPath(u, v), cut = inCut(u, v);
    const col = hl ? C.weak : cut ? C.hull : "currentColor";
    const line = svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", x(p[0]) + ux * r).attr("y1", y(p[1]) + uy * r)
      .attr("x2", x(q[0]) - ux * r).attr("y2", y(q[1]) - uy * r)
      .attr("stroke", col).attr("stroke-width", hl || cut ? 4 : 1.6)
      .attr("stroke-opacity", hl || cut ? 1 : 0.7)
      .attr("marker-end", `url(#${hl ? "mf-p" : cut ? "mf-c" : "mf-n"})`);
    if (hl && dirOf(u, v) < 0) line.attr("stroke-dasharray", "6 4");
    const mx = (x(p[0]) + x(q[0])) / 2 - uy * 16, my = (y(p[1]) + y(q[1])) / 2 + ux * 16;
    svg.append("text").attr("x", mx).attr("y", my + 5).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
       .attr("fill", hl ? C.weak : "currentColor").attr("font-weight", R.flow[j] === k ? 700 : 400)
       .text(`${R.flow[j]}/${k}`);
  });
  for (const [v, p] of Object.entries(mfPos)) {
    svg.append("circle").attr("cx", x(p[0])).attr("cy", y(p[1])).attr("r", 20)
       .attr("fill", "white").attr("fill-opacity", 0.9).attr("stroke", "currentColor").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", x(p[0])).attr("y", y(p[1]) + 6).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
       .attr("fill", "black").text(v);
  }
  return svg.node();
}
```

### How many augmentations?

With integer capacities, each augmentation raises the value by at least 1, so the
algorithm stops; but if the paths are chosen badly, the number of steps can grow with the
size of the capacities. @edmonds1972 showed that always augmenting along a **shortest**
path (fewest arcs) needs a number of augmentations bounded by a polynomial in the number
of nodes and arcs, whatever the capacities. That is the rule used in the figures above.

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: no augmenting path means maximum
Let $S$ be the set of nodes reachable from $s$ in the residual network; $t \notin S$
because there is no augmenting path. Every arc leaving $S$ must be **full**, or its head
would be reachable. Every arc entering $S$ must carry **zero** flow, or cancelling it would
reach its tail. So the value of the flow, which is "flow out of $S$ minus flow into
$S$", equals the capacity of $S$. Since every flow is at most every cut, this flow is
maximum and this cut is minimum, which also proves the max-flow min-cut theorem.

If capacities are integers, the algorithm starts at zero and only ever adds integer
bottlenecks, so it ends with an integer maximum flow.
:::

## In practice

- **Matching and assignment** reduce to max flow; see
  [Matching](../integrality-and-matching/matching.qmd).
- **Minimum cuts** are useful in their own right: the cheapest way to disconnect a
  network, which parts of a system to select under "if you take this you need that"
  rules, and image segmentation (separating foreground from background pixels).
- **Faster algorithms** exist and are what solvers use on huge networks, but the
  augmenting-path picture and the max-flow min-cut certificate are what you need to
  reason about flows.
